q: What two properties must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to be optimal?
options: The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure
A sorted input and unique values
explain: Some optimal solution must begin with the greedy choice, and the remaining problem must be a smaller instance that is solved the same way.

q: In activity selection, which rule gives a maximum set of non-overlapping activities?
options: Repeatedly pick the compatible activity that finishes earliest
Pick the activity that starts earliest
Pick the activity with the fewest overlaps
explain: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest. Shortest-first and earliest-start can both be beaten by counterexamples.

q: Activities (start–finish): a1 1–4, a2 3–5, a3 0–6, a4 5–7, a5 3–9, a6 5–9, a7 6–10, a8 8–11. How many does the greedy algorithm select?
explain: a1 finishes first (4). Then a4 (starts at 5, finishes at 7). Then a8 (starts at 8). No other compatible activity remains.

q: With coins {1, 3, 4}, how many coins does greedy use for amount 6, and what is the optimum?
explain: Greedy grabs the 4 first and has to finish with 1s. This is the smallest amount where greedy fails for this coin system.

q: Greedy coin change (largest coin first) gives the minimum number of coins for every coin system.
explain: False. It works for canonical systems such as Indian rupees, but fails for {1, 3, 4} at 6 and {1, 10, 25} at 30 (greedy 25 + 1×5 uses 6 coins; 10 + 10 + 10 uses 3).

q: What is the time complexity of activity selection on n activities?
options: O(n log n), dominated by sorting by finish time
explain: After sorting, one linear scan picks the activities. If they are already sorted by finish time, it is O(n).

q: One activity finishes at time 5 and another starts at time 5. Are they compatible?
options: Yes: compatibility is start ≥ previous finish
Only if both have the same length
It depends on the greedy rule
explain: Activities are usually half-open intervals [start, finish), so one can begin exactly when another ends.

q: How is the greedy choice for activity selection proved correct?
options: Exchange argument: replace the first activity of an optimal schedule by the earliest-finishing one; the schedule stays valid and the same size
By induction on the number of coins
explain: The earliest-finishing activity ends no later than the one it replaces, so it cannot clash with the later activities.

q: For which problem is the simple greedy rule (best value per unit weight first) optimal?
explain: With fractions allowed, filling with the best ratio first is optimal. For 0/1 knapsack you cannot take part of an item, so dynamic programming (topic 27) is needed.

q: Shortest-activity-first is tried on activities a 0–5, b 4–7, c 6–11. How many does it select, and what is the maximum?
options: It selects 1 (b); the maximum is 2 (a, c)
explain: b is shortest (length 3), but it overlaps both a and c. Earliest-finish picks a, then c.
